claims.claim: Held-out crowd table has 135,630 rows, 52 models, cap 2,713; NBA table has 12,900 rows, 30 teams, cap 258.

Held-out crowd table built from 135,634 raw rows after removing 2 content-overlap rows and 2 rare-participant rows (652 prompt-only overlaps kept); source: derived/task_meta/final_meta.json (copy, name lists removed).

Development tables: Arena 55k 57,477 rows, 64 models (cap 1,150 derived); MT-Bench human 3,355 rows, 6 models (cap 68 derived); sizes from derived/task_meta/search_meta.json (copy, name lists removed).
Recorded removal budgets of the studied configuration: crowd top 62, crowd mid 4 rows; NBA top 62, NBA mid 8 rows; all four flipped within the cap.
Budgets as percent of all comparisons (derived k/N): 0.046%, 0.003%, 0.48%, 0.062%.
Both held-out episodes (seeds 21 and 22) returned identical per-case budgets; the studied configuration's recorded durations were 4.45 s and 4.51 s per episode (hardware not recorded).
Held-out family scores 0.988 (crowd) and 0.864 (sports); overall 0.926; mean k/cap 0.074; flip rate 1.0.
Random-removal reference score 0.041 and influence-only reference score 0.926; the latter equals the held-out overall score.
Random removal flipped 0/20 draws for F1, F3, F4 and 6/20 for F2 (and 7/20 for control F5, 0/20 for F6).

The evaluator-recorded influence-only reference (B2) budgets equal the studied configuration's in all four real cases and both permutation controls (62, 4, 62, 8; 2, 10); B2's construction is unverified and no conclusion depends on it.
Opponent-targeted (B3) budgets: 650, 6, 88, 12 rows for F1 to F4 (ratios to studied 10.5, 1.5, 1.4, 1.5).
Top-pair share ratio sports/crowd is 10.5 and mid-pair ratio is 21.0; the top-pair ratio equals the table-size ratio 135,630/12,900.

Mean comparisons per participant (2N/M) are 5,217 (crowd) and 860 (sports); 62 rows are 1.2% and 7.2% of that (about 6x); mid budgets 0.077% and 0.93% (about 12x); sports has the larger share under both normalisers (10.5x and 21.0x under k/N).
Sports top-pair budget uses 24% of its 258-row cap.
Empty-set control flips no case; cross-table copy control recorded 0 flips in 2 trials; no inference is drawn from the copy control because its construction is not documented.
Permutation controls: moved fraction 0.660 vs expected 0.662 (crowd), 0.498 vs 0.500 (sports); rating-spread ratios 0.088 and 0.160; non-vacuous.
Permuted top pairs flipped with 2 rows (crowd) and 10 rows (sports) versus 62 on real tables; control gap +0.112.

Held-out evaluation status completed with outcome qualified and success indicator true; qualification gate criteria are not recorded in the evidence, so qualified is not read as certifying controls or validity; candidate diagnostics unverified and unused.
Investigation found no winner: three search configurations were scored (3 of 3, 0 unscored), each 0.4993 equal to the starting baseline 0.4993, difference 0.0; selection kind non-winner candidate.
The starting baseline was not run on held-out tables; selected configuration equals the baseline's development score.
Bradley-Terry model extensions and estimation literature described at title level (ties, order effects, multivariate, Bayesian, existence of MLE, ridge, computation).
Sampling-based uncertainty for BT scores and ranks, and growing-parameter asymptotics, are studied in cited work (title-level description).
Broderick et al. propose a finite-sample robustness metric for when dropping a little data changes conclusions.
Chatbot Arena is a crowd-vote platform that aggregates pairwise preferences into rankings.
Influence-function analysis of removing a training point motivates the Newton-step row ordering.

Prior work (title level) studies vote-rigging strategies against Chatbot Arena and their effect on model rankings; our deletion-only setting is not compared numerically and no claim is made about which manipulations that work allows.

Evaluator source for comparators B1-B3 and the controls is not staged; only recorded outcomes (flip counts, budgets, moved fractions, spread ratios, copy flips) are reported and construction details are not claimed. B2 is not asserted to equal any step of the studied configuration.
Broderick et al. is described only as proposing a finite-sample robustness metric for when dropping a little data changes conclusions; no further characterisation is made.
The studied configuration's recorded top-pair budgets are the same number of rows (62) for crowd and sports tables; caps differ (2,713 vs 258); true minima are not established.
Random removal flipped the crowd mid pair in 6 of 20 draws; this suggests but does not establish a small rating gap (gaps not recorded).

The evidence registry records only total scores (0.4993) and per-episode runtimes (about 1.3 s, 2.0 s, 114 s) for the three development configurations; no per-family, per-case or per-comparator development breakdown is recorded, so no claim is made about whether MT-Bench pairs flip.
